review:
These games, particularly Kingdom Hearts 1 & 2, have such a strong, emotional impact on me to the point where it's honestly difficult to put into words how much I adore these games, despite technically having quite a lot of mechanical and narrative flaws. To heavily simplify my thoughts; 

Kingdom Hearts 1 has aged like wine and even thought some of the platforming CAN be janky, it's NOWHERE near the dated/unplayable mess that a lot of people on the internet make it out to be. It also has the most cohesive, straightforward plot that does an excellent job balancing out the Disney content (which don't feel like filler like in the later installments) with the OG content. It's also a comfort game for me, literally all I have to do is listen to some of the music and/or watch a cutscene and my mood uplifts exponentially.

Rechain of Memories has a divisive combat system that can admittedly be broken with the right sleights (looking at you Sonic Blade and Lethal Frame) but I personally loved the strategising and deck building which gave the game an extremely unique flair that's never been replicated since. Also has one of the better plots in the franchise and arguably has Sora at his most complex.

Kingdom Hearts 2 straight up has the best combat system ever in a video game. Not just in the franchise, not just for a Square Enix game, but the best combat system period. Bold claim yes, but one I stand by wholeheartedly. Plot admittedly has a lot of filler sprinkled in between the beginning, middle act, and end game but those moments (particularly the phenomenal and heartwrenching prologue with Roxas) are so well-written and packed with so much emotion that I'm willing to excuse the filler in between.

Birty By Sleep is another divisive game in the collection due to the introduction of the command deck as well as the game that introduced a lot of plot beats/deus ex machinas that have became synonymous with the franchise's controversial perception online, but I still really liked/borderline loved this entry. The command deck I found myself enjoying way more than I thought I would because of how customisable it can make every encounter, but admittedly the inclusion of shotlocks and certain commands (Mega Flare) can trivialise a lot of fights. The game is also packed full with content as it has 3 whole campaigns that can take up to 25 hours to complete if you're going after every collectible, 2 additional stories, an entire mini-game based on Fortune Street that is practically a pseudo game of its own, and a wealth of side objectives for you to collect.

358/2 and ReCoded aren't games but rather movies but I still had a great time watching them. 358/2 is one of the more depressive and mature entry in the series that recontextualises quite a lot of moments in Kingdom Hearts 2 to give them a far more tragic angle. Also has great character building for Roxas who is already one of the more well-written characters in the series. 

ReCoded is clowned on online for having an absolutely baffling plot (yes Nomura, I'm sure it was absolutely necessary for Jiminy's Journal to be its own character to serve the overarching narrative) and while I won't pretend for a millisecond that the plot is in any shape or form cohesive or objectively solid, I cannot deny that I had a lot of fun watching the charming first act that returns to the more simple, whimsical tone that was heavily prevalent in the first installment before moving onto the more dramatic stuff that makes up the second and third act.

Additional notes:
The music for every game is absolutely god-tier. Tracks that range from serene (both versions of Twilight Town) to thrilling (Hand to Hand), to melancholic (Roxas's theme) to daunting but encouraging (the final boss theme in Kingdom Hearts 1 which in my opinion is one of the best themes in all of gaming), there is also Simple & Clean and Sanctuary which are perfectly complimented by Hikaru Utada's powerful vocals. This is Yoko Shimomura at her absolute finest which is saying a lot because she's well-regarded by practically everyone in the gaming sphere for being one of the most legenday composers in the gaming industry. 

While some of the terminology can be kind of confusing on your first playthrough and some moments in certain games will have you doing a double take or scratching your head (Birth by Sleep and ReCoded are the worst offenders for this), the overarching narrative is honestly nowhere near as confusing as people make it out to be. I feel like a lot of people either A) don't pay attention to the cutscenes because they're too busy laughing at the Disney characters doing conventionally anime stuff or B) just watch purposefully out-of-context videos on YouTube or hyper exaggerated summary videos on YouTube that play up the more ridiculous moments in the plot to showcase "how crazy Kingdom Hearts" is. Also unlike before, most of the games are available in one bundle and don't require you to go scouting out 4 different handheld systems to get the full experience so the old argument of "it's stupid that the plot is spread throughout all of these platforms" no longer holds any water.

Not to be a gaming elitist that goes by a mantra of "easy/normal mode doesn't make you a real gamer, hard mode is the only legit way to play a game" but I do think, once you've gotten a grasp of the mechanics of course, you should play Kingdom Hearts games on Proud and Critical (especially KH2) to get the most worthwhile experience with them. Proud and Critical mode makes you engage with the games MANY mechanics in several ways that is almost never necessary in the easier difficulty settings and it really shines a new light on just how complex but fine-tuned these games really are.

Sora is the best protagonist in all of gaming and I will die on that hill.

No matter how "anime, power of friendship cringe" these games are, they provide me with an experience that almost no other IP can offer me. The gameplay, plot, characters and music all combine together to a product that is practically magic in my eyes. These games are peak content in my eyes and no amount of "but they're so cringy, Mickey holds a sword for god's sake" from people online will ever make me reconsider my statement.

Kingdom Hearts 1.5+2.5 is a massive collection of four HD remasters of Kingdom Hearts games and the cutscenes of 358/2 Days and Re:Coded remastered. Now why just the cutscenes and not the full games? Because the two DS games ran completely different engines and honestly, were not good gameplay wise. Storywise 358/2 Days is an absolute tearjerker but actually playing the DS original sucked hard, so only the cutscenes being remastered is a blessing in disguise so you can get the feels and important story beats and then immediately get back to the fun. (Trust me I'll explain why later in the review)

The games in question are the two numbered titles Kingdom Hearts 1 Final Mix and Kingdom Hearts 2 Final Mix, and Re:Chain of Memories and Birth by Sleep Final Mix. What does Final Mix mean? Well those games released back before DLC existed so Final Mix just means the definitive versions with quality of life changes and new content, so if you played these games in your childhood back during the PS2 it's a must buy as they made so many good changes (most notably the ability to skip cutscenes in KH1 PRAISE GOD!)

Tested on Steam Deck and the games all work perfectly with 5 hours of battery life on a single charge. All the games in the collection are running on the old PS2 era engine the series is primarily known for, so they're not demanding games and can pretty much run on any modern PC, including non-gaming PCs.

Now with all this said, there's an important warning I gotta give for newcomers, and it's regarding the Kingdom Hearts Conundrum™. For longtime fans you know exactly what I'm talking about. You see, the Kingdom Hearts franchise is absolutely magical and all must plays, however they have a big flaw, and that's that the story is absolutely complicated and requires knowledge of previous games to make sense. And I'm not talking just mainline numbered titles, I mean ALL TITLES. Kingdom Hearts 2 for example has key story points that were explained in Chain of Memories which at the time was a spinoff title on a completely different system, that being the Nintendo Game Boy Advanced. Birth By Sleep especially contained a lot of important story details and that was a spinoff on the PlayStation Portable. And of course 358/2 Days originally being on the Nintendo DS and having really controversial gameplay elements that really make it not as inviting. 

Nowadays it's not so bad because we got the collections, but as you continue your Kingdom Hearts journeys you HAVE to play the games by order of release as they were designed that way. Trust me as a Kingdom Hearts fan since the beginning, you cannot skip any of them otherwise trying to piece everything together is just gonna hurt your head. The good news is you don't have to play every single one. Re:Chain of Memories you can just watch the cutscenes on Youtube as the gameplay is mainly just supplemental. Birth by Sleep though, strongly recommended to play because it's story is deeply important and it's gameplay really damn good.

Barring the Kingdom Hearts pain train, you don't need to know anything to have fun, and that's what Kingdom Hearts is, just pure fun. A grand crossover adventure between Final Fantasy and Disney that on paper shouldn't work but it does, with great actions, great moments, and overall just games that will stick with you for the rest of your life. There's a reason this franchise is so beloved the world over.

If you want to know more, the Youtuber SuperButterBuns has made a series called Kingdom Hearts For Beginners that will give you lots of tips tricks and headsup to make your journey more enjoyable. https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLaDEzrYRlCgFhp2F8wFfNWEx1Y6qbMQZu

These are my favorite games of all time, flaws and all. I was so excited to finally get to play them on my Steam Deck all cozy in bed. Imagine my disappointment when I realize not only are these "new" ports still just as unstable as they were on EGS, but they somehow made them worse. I'm gonna list below issues specific to the Steam Deck, this new port, and then legacy issues from the EGS version that need to be fixed before I can recommend these versions.

STEAM DECK ISSUES:
  -  Audio crackles on my non OLED Steam Deck whenever a BGM is playing. Its distracting and awful to listen to.
  -  The screen squashes when using the native 16:10 800p resolution, making the feature of supporting the resolution useless.

New Issues:
  -  The AI upscaled textures look truly awful and lack any polish. Any time a texture contains any type of shading thats supposed to create depth or a shadow is completely flattened, All dithered patterns that are supposed to create a gradient are deep fried and create a zit pattern instead.
  -  Some models now load the incorrect textures.
  -  The whole selling point of this version were the textures and theyre awful. Please give the option to downgrade to the older textures.

Legacy Issues
  -  Instability. The game does not handle alt tabbing or framerates higher than 60 well. The games can crash easily resulting in hours of progress potentially being lost or corrupting saves.
  -  The fullscreen mode is pointless as the second you alt tab it switches back to windowed mode.
  -  Many sound effects are broken and lack reverb like Xigbar's guns.
  -  The game's frametime delivery system is just broken. If you try to use gsync the game is a suttery mess. If you disable it the game can still stutter on loads.
  -  The higher framerate options above 60 are worthless not just because of increased instability, but because some objects when rendered on screen force the game back down to 60 anyway.

These are the main issues but there are others like COM lacking its alt control options or it still lacking basic additions like dual audio or cutscenes above 30 fps, but those I can stand recommending without. The main issues I listed NEED to be addressed. Most of them have needed to be for THREE YEARS on EGS. Please dont leave the games I love in this state

Kingdom Hearts 1.5 has always been a special game to me. A true favorite. Because of its music, its story, its characters… but also because of the moment in life when I first discovered it.

I still remember borrowing the PlayStation 2 box from my big sister whenever she went to work. I would put the CD back exactly how it was—same angle, same tiny dust mark on the corner—just to make sure she wouldn’t notice. Those were the golden days.

Today, I’m older. My tastes have evolved, my gaming hours are more limited. And yet, in June 2024, the Integrum Masterpiece collection suddenly drops on Steam. Every game in the saga. (Except the latest one, Chains of Melody, still missing in action.) And just like that, the door to light opens again in my life—ready to pull me out of the darkness.

So here it is: my review of the achievements in KH1.5.

KH1.5 has 55 achievements, and there’s something for everyone: completing the main story, finding all the collectibles, collecting every piece of equipment, reaching level 100, finishing every challenge, every boss, every mini-game... and much more. It’s a JRPG, so of course—it demands time, patience, and a healthy dose of madness. Expect around 130 hours for the full 100%. I did it in 46, but hey, pro gamer privilege.

You’ll probably start on Beginner Mode for your first run. It’s perfect to learn the mechanics, enjoy the story, and ease into the game without too much frustration. The first 20 hours? Probably some of the best you’ll ever experience. You’ll save entire worlds, meet iconic characters, and defeat thousands of Heartless. And once the adventure ends... the real grind begins.

You’ll need to hit level 100—either with optimized EXP gear or pure brute force. You’ll have to fight secret bosses like the Clock Tower Phantom, with sadistic but brilliant mechanics. Complete all the tournaments in Olympus: in teams, solo, timed... across four brackets. Hunt rare drops from Heartless to craft powerful items with the synthesis system. And let’s not forget the special Heartless, each with their own unique quirks—definitely bring a guide for those.

Like every classic JRPG, KH1.5 throws a ton of collectibles at you: the 99 Dalmatians, the Trio Marks, Ansem’s Reports, the Winnie the Pooh mini-games, all the magic spells, the hidden chests, the abilities... You’ll revisit every world again and again. But that’s part of the beauty. The repetition becomes ritual.

Then comes Proud Mode. The expert difficulty. That’s when the tears begin to fall. I’ve never struggled so much in my life as a trophy hunter. Maybe because I didn’t have much JRPG experience. Maybe because I always rushed Kingdom Hearts. I had to learn every enemy’s pattern, optimize every stat, manage my items with care, and above all—stop yelling at Donald for wasting his damn MP. It’s brutal.

And then comes the final madness. Finish the game in under 15 hours, without dying once, using only the default equipment. It’s doable after completing Proud Mode. But your damage output is a joke.

And after all that... welcome to the KH1.5 100% club. Even if I suffered, it’s a journey I’d do again. Again and again. Just to feel that warm nostalgia. That passion for Kingdom Hearts. And for gaming as a whole.

Thanks for reading. And good luck, fellow Keyblade wielder.

Coming back to Kingdom Hearts 1 after playing it as a kid, I was surprised by how much more depth the game has than I remembered. The combat is not just about mashing X, bosses require paying attention, learning patterns, managing abilities, and actually thinking about your approach. Some fights were much harder than I remembered, but in a satisfying way.

The characters, worlds, music, and story are still the biggest strengths of the game. There is something special about seeing Disney and Final Fantasy elements come together in a way that somehow works, and the emotional moments still hit even years later.

That being said, the game crashing after certain boss fights is extremely frustrating, it can ruin the flow of a playthrough, and it does when it happens. The camera can also be a major problem, especially during the Dark Sora fight where it can make an already difficult battle feel worse. Lock on can also randomly stop working or ignore enemies, which leads to some frustrating moments.

Despite those problems, I had a great time replaying Kingdom Hearts. The combat is deeper than I remembered, the adventure is still memorable, and the story continues to be one of the most unique crossover ideas in gaming.

Looking forward to continuing the series and seeing what comes next.

Kingdom Hearts is a game series that has been with me for almost my entire life, so when the collection finally came to Steam, I felt the obligation to fully complete this series once and for all, to truly grasp my feelings on this absurd concept of an IP (and attempt to fit it all in a single review... well, three reviews).

To start off, a constant in every game is the utterly phenomenal soundtrack by Yoko Shimomura. Her works are probably the most iconic part of the series and are easily the greatest feature of them. Even in the most seemingly mundane part of any given game, the music accompanying it elevates it beyond the sum of its parts and makes it far more memorable than it really has any right to be. This series is one of the catalysts for my love of video game soundtracks and, despite any complaints I may have with any game listed in this review, the music will always be a positive, with almost no exceptions.

[b]Kingdom Hearts Final Mix[/b] is one of the two most popular installments, with those two probably being the only ones most will play out of this collection. KH1 is a classic for a lot of people, and on replay all these years later, still holds up decently well. This is the simplest and most grounded story in the series, and holds up as a standalone. The stakes are well-defined and Sora's goals are clear-cut. In terms of exploration, KH1 is an outlier compared to practically the entire series in that there is no minimap system, and worlds have layouts that aren't entirely linear. Paired with the game rarely ever giving you explicit directions on where to go, it can be confusing on where to go during a first playthrough. For some, this is a positive, and others, a negative. Exploration and intrigue is a key part of KH1's design philosophy, so unless you look up walkthroughs, there's really no getting around this point. Many areas have tiny little secrets that could take several playthroughs to find, some of which I first found even on my most recent run. It's a gameplay experience you won't find in any future installments, so it's a unique aspect that this title alone holds. As for combat, it's apparent that the action RPG system was still finding its footing, but it's still solid enough to not be a total detriment. Attacks have weight to them and Sora is extremely grounded, leading to aerial fights feeling disadvantageous. Enemies themselves are generally simple, having a couple attacks and maybe some resistances and weaknesses, but elite enemies found in the late game can provide a challenge, especially in groups (which they will be in, often). Bosses on the other hand are where the bulk of the game's difficulty will come from, with a few notorious fights feeling almost out of place with the movement options you have. Overall, KH1 has its issues, and can be frustrating at times, but is an enjoyable experience at the end. I wouldn't say this is my favorite installment, but it is by far the most unique, and to this day, no other installment has captured the feeling this one has.

[b]Kingdom Hearts Re:Chain of Memories[/b] is a PS2 remake of a GBA game, remastered for modern systems. Re:CoM is the first game to deviate from the core aRPG gameplay (and won't be the last), delving into a card-based battle system. Combat is similar to KH1, but with every action tied to cards with numerical values, that must be higher than your opponents in order to connect, or else they will be deflected and leave you open to attack. This system is one of the most contested in the series, with the on-the-fly strategy required sometimes feeling unfair, especially in the late game. At the same time, the system is also easily exploited, with certain combos of cards trivializing most fights. The world system itself has also turned into cards, with each world being a re-hash of KH1 worlds. These worlds are made up of preset generic rooms you create with even more cards, and their stories round up to being quick one-note summaries of the originals. The main focus of the story is Sora and Riku, dealing with the internal conflicts within their memories, while also dealing with the external conflicts of what will be the main antagonists of the next game. Re:CoM was made to be a bridge between KH1 and KH2, and story-wise fills that role very well, with it being the highlight of the experience. Otherwise, the game is fairly average, with a passable gameplay concept, but a repetitive loop.

[b]Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix[/b] is contending with KH1 for most popular game and is a return to form. If you were to ask any single fan of the series which game was their favorite, if they didn't say KH1, they would probably say KH2. KH2's story picks up where KH Re:CoM left off, and introduces more elements to the story to set up the worldbuilding needed for later installments, namely Nobodies and the ever-looming Organization XIII. The story focuses more on these original concepts compared to KH1, and has a few outstanding highlights, but is generally on the lesser side compared to the previous 2 games. KH2 is radically different from 1 in a few ways, mainly straying away from exploration to focus more on combat. Worlds in KH2 are generally much more linear, with very little deviance in the main path. Treasures and collectibles are usually not too far from where you'll naturally go, and what you can't reach on your first visit is usually just obtained with movement options you unlock later in the game. This world design makes for clearer objectives, but erases any amount of discovery the game could have. What KH2 makes up for this is in its combat, which is the main highlight of this game. Combat in KH2 is fast, fluid, and flashy, and the addition of Reaction Commands and Drive Forms make for spectacles of fights from beginning to end. Enemies themselves are also much more dynamic, with many having attacks that can now combo and cover much more ground. Bosses are more well-rounded compared to KH1, and the endgame lets you test your mastery of the mechanics, though with a few exploits. KH2 is a game with a handful of glaring flaws, but I still admit I have a soft spot for it.

[b]Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep Final Mix[/b] was originally a PSP game with a multiplayer aspect. The game was remastered and the multiplayer shaved off to be a singleplayer experience. This game acts as a prequel to all previous games and lays the groundwork for Integrum Masterpiece's main antagonist, as well as worldbuilding for the universe and the rules of the Keyblade. The game is split into 3 parts, with you controlling 3 different characters and experiencing their perspective of the story. This leads to each character's individual personality feeling a bit flat, but the overarching narrative makes up for it by the end. Worlds are smaller and more tightly packed, but are divided up for each character's visit, meaning you can't see the entirety of most worlds from just one character's POV. Combat is mix of the numbered games' action and Re:CoM's deckbuilding, and strikes a mix that on revisit is much better than what I first saw it as. It provides a good amount of strategy while still allowing leeway for simple action. The deck system can still be abused greatly to decimate most of the game, but the amount of commands available still allow for freedom in your gameplay style. The difficulty in this game is a steep increase, with some bosses feeling almost unfair in their attacks (and a certain boss [i]actually[/i] being unfair). while enemies are just basic. BBS is divisive in almost every aspect, but I came to enjoy it more than before.

And to footnote the last two for completion because I'm running out of space, [b]358/2 Days and Re:Coded[/b] are just remastered collections of cutscenes with no gameplay. Days is the more enjoyable one by far with more overall plot importance. If you care for understanding the whole story of this series, I'd recommend watching them... but maybe skim Re:Coded.

This is a [u]non story spoiler review[/u] of these games, they will be reviewed as a whole rather than the individual titles.

[u]Introduction[/u]
Kingdom Hearts changed my life. I'm not kidding. I did not grow up with this series, I only got into it when I purchased it in June 2024. I had also never played a game by Square Enix before (not even Final Fantasy) so I had no previous biases or opinions towards that. But where I'm standing now I can confidently say this game changed my life.

Before getting into the series I really only played a handful of single player games, it's not that I hated them but I was never able to form an attachment to the characters I was seeing and the gameplay didn't excite me. Before getting these games I just didn't broaden my horizons on video games much because I didn't know there was any way to tell a compelling story in the medium of games. Sure there were a few but I never actually wanted to PLAY the games, I preferred to watch them on YouTube like a movie or show. But as many gamers may tell you, watching a game is so different than actually PLAYING it, that was something I was unaware of at the time.

So skip to 2024, a friend of mine tells me to purchase the games since they finally became available on steam. I had no real interest in them since I saw Goofy and Donald Duck and immediately saw it as a childish game with no real emotion. Which is a fair assumption to make at first, but it isn't until you peel back the many layers that you get to the real meat of the story and characters. The characters and their interactions are what really make this game special to me. Ironically, the game has so much heart to it. It was if my eyes were being opened to a new world for the first time, and while this may seem dramatic to many people over an anime Disney game, I can't find another way to describe the feeling. The pure whimsical and dramatic nature of these games is amazing.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Most might be familiar with gameplay like this, I don't really know the correct terms for it but I know it's an action JRPG with real time combat. The only exception to this is RE: Chain of Memories, which is more of a card game. I really love the gameplay, as someone who literally never played a game similar to this in my life I had a blast. Learning the combat at first was definitely challenging and I won't pretend like it was easy, but as you keep playing more and more of the games it gets way easier as they implement new systems to keep things fresh. There are plenty of ways to stun lock enemies which was great for me personally, though it's not that easy so if you prefer a challenge don't be afraid that you're going to do it on accident. Speaking of challenge, this game can be VERY hard when it wants to, I think most of it is accidental due to how old this game is and trying to run it at 60 FPS when it was made for 30 but even with a few bugs here and there it still works. 

From what my friend who grew up with these games has told me, Square Enix is pretty much known for having terrible PC ports of their games which is a shame. I hope in the future they're able to port these games properly so they don't have so many bugs. In most cases I recommend playing these games at 60 or 30 FPS. Do not go over that even if your monitor can handle it, the game seems to freak out and mess with cutscene speed when you do. Crashing wasn't an issue with me personally besides one or two instances but I know that's a problem some people experience, there are plenty of fixes online to help you if you run into that problem though.

[u]Conclusion[/u]
I hope this review was at least somewhat helpful for someone. Especially those who don't really play video games a lot, or are new to RPG's. Since playing through the whole Kingdom Hearts series I moved onto Final Fantasy and I've nearly finished playing every single numbered title. And it's all because of these games, if my friend hadn't suggested them to me and I hadn't bought them I probably would've still interacted with video games in the same way that I did. So thank you Square Enix, for creating such a memorable experience for not just me but thousands of people around the world.

Ah, the beautiful baby of the Disney-Squenix love affair. The Kingdom Hearts franchise is an interesting one. First off, credit where it's due: for the time KH1 originally came out, it was kind of earth-shattering. Even by today's standard, the combat system is fun and challenging with great scaling almost all the way through level 80 or so. The music and atmosphere was also next tier. Definitely pretty corny and cliche with the story-telling that was mostly pretty weak, but at the time, that was more than acceptable. Definitely revolutionized combat systems for these styles of games. With over 20 years of age, though, KH1's short-comings really stain its glorious legacy: bad story-writing, annoying platforming, targeting and control mechanics that really don't facilitate the hardest difficulty on the game. Game's a lot better if you skip all the cutscenes, assuming you know where you're supposed to go.

Re:Chain is bad. I don't even want to talk about. The progression and scaling in the game is all badly paced, the card-based combat system is more annoying than anything, and the navigation... eh, it just all feels like a slog. The story's not too bad with Riku's story definitely stealing the show, but... this ain't it.

KH2 is definitely the best game in the whole franchise. The story-telling is still plenty cliche at some parts, but at others, it's actually deeply moving and engaging, somber and emotional. Sure, the pacing of an extremely long prolong is a little weird, but it's totally okay because Roxas is probably the best character in the entire franchise. And the combat and music all got dialed up a couple notches. Stupendous game that not only continues the tradition of fun power-scaling and epic super-boss fights, but freakin' smashes it to pieces.

358/2 days is definitely the best-told story in the entire franchise, and one of the best-told JRPG stories of all time. Simple set up, small main cast with tons of chemistry (thank you, Axel), powerful villain, and the world-building lends itself so well to the story-telling, it's kind of shame it detracts from the stories of the other games in the franchise. Leads to some extremely emotional and powerful moments in the story. Never played the actual game though. Would have liked to.

BBS is another great KH game. Story-telling again is a little cliche and weak except for a few parts that hit pretty well. Combat is a ton of fun, with the command form mechanic really stealing the show. The balance in the game is pretty bad, though. Aqua is just objectively the best character, some command forms just straight up nerf your character, and the grinding in the game is next-level slooooow, especially on the hardest difficulty, so don;t even think about maxing out your characters. With some good skill, you can 100% the game, including super-bosses, with a lv 40 Aqua on critical.

Re-Coded is not a good story. If you're going to enter it into the game as a story only, I'm going to judge it as a story only, and it is 90% wasted. There are two useful things that happen in this story: (1) Sora (supposedly) learns and connects with the pain and heartache of the people connected to him--people like Roxas and Ventus. Except that the story brushes through this so quickly, it doesn't feel genuine, and besides that, this is just data-Sora--not even the real Sora. So it was another failed opportunity to fix one of the biggest problems with the story-telling in the franchise, and that is that Sora is just too dang happy-go-lucky. I'm not convinced he knows what real loss feels like, even though he definitely had a dark-ish moment at the midpoint of KH2. It's frustrating, because I don't feel like he's fully emotionally invested in the stakes of the franchise. Anyhow, I ramble. The other thing this game is supposed to do is (2) set up a possibility to save all the characters that are connected to him and that are counting on him to help them. It was alluded to in BBS, but this game spells it out quite clearly and shows that there is definitely going to be an effort to do that. That's actually kind of nice, but the issue is all this stuff happens in the finale of the game. The rest of the story is utterly wasted.

All in all, though, I'm still very impressed and get a lot of fun out of the combat system of these games. Combat is definitely where this franchise shines. There's just a good flow to it: your character can close the distance and attack pretty easily in most instances, learning enemy attack patterns sets you up for powerful counters, strategizing your abilities can let you unleash massive damage, forms are just satisfying, and it all feels immensely rewarding when you get the mechanics down. Pity about the current state of the franchise, but most of the games in this bundle are definitely worth the play-through, especially KH2 and BBS. And with the bundle that often goes on sale, it's a staggeringly good value.
